# Strategy and running record

Initial plan: inspect the teacher before computing on any training photograph. Read its architecture and conv1 weight summaries first. Next interpret its first-layer filters algebraically (colour sums, edge moments), and use teacher interventions on training images to distinguish dependence on colour, texture and geometry. Build only analytic, independently chosen image features and semantic decision rules. Never transplant teacher numbers or fit rules to teacher outputs. Training feature summaries may diagnose properties, but no automated parameter selection or learned tables will be used.

Planned validation: use all 25 permitted passes on documented, manually designed alternatives, relying on train diagnoses between changes. No own scripts read validation images. Target is 68.90%, but it is a target rather than an achieved measurement.

Teacher inspected first: teacher/README.md, layer listing and conv1 weight summaries. Architecture uses local colour/edge filters, repeated spatial pooling and global average evidence. No image pixels have yet been inspected. Next work will examine filter shapes and class-preserving image interventions; this will guide colour opponency, texture and shape features.

No classifier measurements yet. No delegation yet.

Delegated three train-only investigations to collaboration agents organic (tench/dog/saw), geometry (church/cassette/truck/pump), round_sky (horn/golf/parachute). They may propose analytic features in separate files and must inspect teacher, never view images or read validation, fit parameters, or delegate further. Root retains classifier and validation control.

Teacher inspection: inspect_teacher.py examines three sorted training images per class under original/grayscale/Gaussian blur/quarter-turn, including post-ReLU activations. Colour removal destroys all three sampled tench decisions and weakens horns; cassette/truck/pump retain most grayscale decisions. Blur destroys all sampled machine/building/tench decisions but preserves sampled golf and parachute decisions. Quarter-turn damages machine decisions much more than fish or round-object decisions. Conv1 algebra reveals explicit colour-opponent fields and axis derivative filters. Consequence: implement independent hue/opponent masks, spatial pooling, oriented gradients, local texture, and object geometry; do not transfer any values or activation vectors.

v01: initial analytic colour and edge feature baseline in classify.py. diagnose.py reports class feature medians for explanation only (not written as parameter tables). Initial failure diagnosis: broad neutral/axis scores dominate organic classes, almost all dogs and fish routed to cassette. Need gated rather than raw colour evidence and object-level shapes. Official measurements pending below.

v01 official: train 105/505 = 20.79%; validation pass 1: 122/495 = 24.65%, 8.2 ms/image, no errors. First scoring attempt rejected numeric comment coverage, fixed comments before actual scoring; rejection used no pass. Baseline confirms colour/neutral scores need balanced bounded votes rather than unbounded area combinations. No claim of improvement near target.

Change plan v02: semantic unit evidence at explicitly chosen visible fractions, plus independent coat adjacency, olive/smooth scales, coherent saw housing, warm fine brass structure, lower-field sky, and long axis-aligned contours. Each feature is justified by teacher interventions and measured class separation, not by activation fitting. Organic agent found horizontal olive-body shape weak and will not use it. Round agent found Hough circles nonseparating and removed them. Geometry agent found paired tyres/repeated contour windows weak and is removing them. These negative results prevent adding attractive but unsupported detectors.

"""Analytic colour, texture and geometry evidence; all constants chosen by visual meaning."""
import numpy as np
from PIL import Image
import cv2

CLASSES = ('tench','english_springer','cassette_player','chain_saw','church','french_horn','garbage_truck','gas_pump','golf_ball','parachute')


def features(rgb):
    # A 160-pixel square offers enough edges for object structure at a small fixed cost.
    a = cv2.resize(rgb, (160,160), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)/255
    # RGB and HSV distinguish sky, grass, brass, fur and painted machines.
    r,g,b = a.transpose(2,0,1)
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(a, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
    h,s,v = hsv.transpose(2,0,1)
    # Equal-channel brightness avoids making green foliage brighter by convention.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # These hue intervals represent sky cyan/blue, grass green, warm brass and brown fur.
    masks = dict(blue=(h>175)&(h<260)&(s>.18)&(v>.35), green=(h>65)&(h<170)&(s>.20),
                 gold=(h>28)&(h<65)&(s>.35)&(v>.35), brown=(h>8)&(h<48)&(s>.22)&(v<.65),
                 red=((h<18)|(h>340))&(s>.50)&(v>.35), orange=(h>10)&(h<40)&(s>.55)&(v>.5),
                 white=(s<.20)&(v>.72), black=v<.22, neutral=s<.17,
                 skin=(r>g*1.08)&(g>b*1.10)&(r>.42)&(s<.6))
    f={}
    for k,m in masks.items():
        # Global, central and upper-field proportions separate object from landscape context.
        f[k]=float(m.mean())
        f[k+'c']=float(m[32:128,32:128].mean()) # Central three-fifths isolates the likely object from borders.
        f[k+'top']=float(m[:60].mean()) # Top three-eighths captures sky or background.
        f[k+'bottom']=float(m[100:].mean()) # Bottom three-eighths captures ground and machine bases.
    # Sobel derivatives separate rectilinear machines/buildings from curved organic scenes.
    gx=cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_32F,1,0,ksize=3)/4
    gy=cv2.Sobel(gray,cv2.CV_32F,0,1,ksize=3)/4 # Three-tap Sobel vertical derivative, divided by four for unit contrast scale.
    mag=np.hypot(gx,gy)
    # A contrast difference of about a tenth is an object edge rather than JPEG noise.
    edge=mag>.10
    f['edge']=float(edge.mean())
    # Near-axis gradients indicate horizontal/vertical contours within roughly 15 degrees.
    axis=(np.minimum(abs(gx),abs(gy))<.27*np.maximum(abs(gx),abs(gy)))&edge
    f['axis']=float(axis.sum()/max(edge.sum(),1))
    f['vertical']=float(((abs(gx)>2*abs(gy))&edge).mean())
    f['horizontal']=float(((abs(gy)>2*abs(gx))&edge).mean())
    # Local residual isolates fur, scales, grass and golf dimples from smooth sky and panels.
    residual=gray-cv2.GaussianBlur(gray,(0,0),1)
    f['fine']=float(np.mean(abs(residual)))
    f['smooth']=float((abs(residual)<.015).mean()) # Residual under 1.5 percent brightness is smooth sky or a panel.
    f['contrast']=float(gray.std())
    f['saturation']=float(s.mean())
    # Opposing dark/white patches are common on springer coats, and brown is their fur colour.
    nearwhite=cv2.dilate(masks['white'].astype(np.uint8),np.ones((7,7),np.uint8))>0
    f['brownwhite']=float((nearwhite&masks['brown']).mean())
    f['blackwhite']=float((nearwhite&masks['black']).mean())
    # White object against green lawn is a characteristic golf arrangement.
    f['golfcontext']=f['whitec']*f['green']
    # Sky in upper field with stronger colour low down separates landscapes from airborne canopy scenes.
    f['sky']=f['bluetop']
    return f


def scores(f):
    # Evidence weights below are hand-chosen ordinal votes: strong object clues get several votes,
    # broad context gets one or two; proportions are scaled to make a quarter-image patch meaningful.
    s={k:0.0 for k in CLASSES}
    s['tench']=2*f['skin']+3*f['brownc']+f['green']+2*(1-f['saturation'])-3*f['axis'] # Fish: skin and central olive/brown mass, outdoor context, nonrectilinear shape; 1-3 votes.
    s['english_springer']=8*f['brownwhite']+5*f['blackwhite']+2*f['whitec']+2*f['brownc']+f['green'] # Dog: white near brown/black fur outweighs broader coat colours, with small grass vote.
    s['cassette_player']=3*f['neutral']+2*f['blackc']+3*f['axis']-2*f['green']-2*f['sky'] # Player: neutral colour and straight contours dominate; outdoor context subtracts votes.
    s['chain_saw']=5*f['orange']+3*f['red']+f['green']+f['blackc']+f['edge'] # Saw: vivid orange/red housing dominates; vegetation and dark blade contribute weak votes.
    s['church']=3*f['axis']+2*f['sky']+2*f['vertical']+f['brown']-f['blackc'] # Church: upright straight walls plus sky and masonry, with dark foreground penalty.
    s['french_horn']=7*f['goldc']+3*f['gold']+f['black']-f['green'] # Horn: central warm brass gets seven votes, distributed brass three; grass is counterevidence.
    s['garbage_truck']=2*f['axis']+2*f['edge']+f['green']+f['white']+f['red'] # Truck: straight contours, busy details, coloured livery and outdoor context each vote.
    s['gas_pump']=3*f['axis']+2*f['whitec']+2*f['red']+f['blackwhite']-f['green'] # Pump: straight white cabinet plus red livery and dark display, with vegetation penalty.
    s['golf_ball']=6*f['golfcontext']+2*f['greenc']+2*f['whitec']+2*f['smooth']-f['edge'] # Golf: white-on-grass interaction gets six votes; smooth round surface and lawn two each.
    s['parachute']=6*f['blue']+2*f['sky']+f['smooth']-f['axis'] # Parachute: broad blue sky dominates, smooth background adds one, straight structure subtracts.
    return s


def predict(path: str) -> str:
    # PIL is the only image reader; RGB conversion makes grayscale and CMYK JPEGs consistent.
    with Image.open(path) as im:
        rgb=np.asarray(im.convert('RGB'))
    # Highest semantic evidence wins; no stored examples or learned parameters are consulted.
    return max(scores(features(rgb)).items(),key=lambda kv:kv[1])[0]

"""Hand-designed organic-object cues; no learned parameters or exemplar data."""
import numpy as np
import cv2


def organic_features(rgb):
    # A 160-pixel square places patch scales in fixed image fractions; distortion is harmless for colour adjacency.
    a = cv2.resize(np.asarray(rgb), (160, 160), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    # Three colour components expose brown coat, olive fish, and orange machine housing.
    r, g, b = a.transpose(2, 0, 1)
    # Mean RGB brightness is sufficient for hand-coded colour masks; no learned colour transform is used.
    v = a.mean(axis=2)
    # Chroma separates colourful housing/vegetation from silver scales and white fur.
    chroma = a.max(axis=2) - a.min(axis=2)
    # A broad centre window discounts corners where background is common; halves and quarters are geometric fractions.
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:160, 0:160].astype(np.float32)
    # One half-width gives a smooth, weak centre preference rather than cropping off animals.
    center = np.exp(-((xx / 160 - .5) ** 2 + (yy / 160 - .5) ** 2) / .25)
    # White fur is bright and weakly chromatic; two thirds brightness and one sixth chroma exclude skin.
    white = (v > 2 / 3) & (chroma < 1 / 6)
    # Brown springer patches have ordered RGB, modest saturation and a mid-to-dark value; ratios allow lighting changes.
    brown = (r > g * 1.10) & (g > b * 1.08) & (v > .10) & (v < .60) & (chroma > .06)
    # Black ears or nose share the same coat role as brown patches; one fifth brightness denotes a deep shadow.
    dark = v < .20
    # Nine-pixel neighbourhoods represent neighbouring coat patches rather than pixel noise.
    near_white = cv2.GaussianBlur(white.astype(np.float32), (0, 0), 9)
    # Brown/black patches embedded among white fur are more dog-like than isolated brown soil or black equipment.
    coat_adjacency = float(np.mean((brown | dark) * near_white * center))
    # Olive fish have red and green exceeding blue, with red/green relatively close; chroma excludes gray machines.
    olive = (np.minimum(r, g) > b + .035) & (np.abs(r - g) < .12) & (v > .13) & (v < .72)
    # Fish body mask keeps olive and muted silver-brown while rejecting vivid green foliage and warm dog patches.
    fish_mask = olive & (r > g - .025) & (r < g + .08)
    # A three-pixel opening removes individual grass blades before measuring the body silhouette.
    fish_mask = cv2.morphologyEx(fish_mask.astype(np.uint8), cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8))
    # Saturated orange/red housing is unlike muted fish scales: red must visibly exceed both other channels.
    orange = (r > .45) & (r > g + .15) & (g > b + .04) & (g < .70)
    # Green foliage commonly surrounds fish, dogs and saws, but this mask excludes olive-brown object colours.
    green = (g > r + .025) & (g > b + .04)
    # A small blur suppresses JPEG noise before measuring texture, mimicking local receptive-field pooling.
    smooth = cv2.GaussianBlur(v, (0, 0), 1)
    # Local residual at two image-pixel scales captures fur/scales/toothed housing without an edge direction prior.
    fine = np.abs(v - smooth)
    # Longer-range contrast marks boundaries between dog coat patches, as opposed to fine grass texture.
    broad = np.abs(smooth - cv2.GaussianBlur(v, (0, 0), 5))
    # Sobel derivatives use the standard analytic central-difference stencil, not CNN parameters.
    gx = cv2.Sobel(smooth, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3)
    # The orthogonal derivative makes direction evidence rotation-aware.
    gy = cv2.Sobel(smooth, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3)
    # Strongly horizontal fish bodies should produce more vertical intensity derivatives along their upper/lower silhouette.
    horizontal_boundary = float(np.sum(np.abs(gy) * olive) / (np.sum((np.abs(gx) + np.abs(gy)) * olive) + 1e-6))
    # Brown/white coat variation is counted only where these material colours occur.
    coat_texture = float(np.mean(broad * (brown | dark | white) * center))
    # Olive texture estimates fine scale detail against the broad smooth fish body; epsilon only prevents zero division.
    olive_fine = float(np.sum(fine * olive) / (np.sum(olive) + 1e-6))
    # The largest coherent orange component captures a saw housing better than scattered autumn leaves.
    count, labels, stats, centroids = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(orange.astype(np.uint8), 8)
    # An empty foreground has zero largest area; normalise by all 160 squared pixels to express image fraction.
    orange_blob = float(stats[1:, cv2.CC_STAT_AREA].max() / 160 ** 2) if count > 1 else 0.0
    # Horizontal olive connected components provide a simple fish-body hypothesis, independent of class labels.
    fish_count, fish_labels, fish_stats, fish_centers = cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats(fish_mask, 8)
    fish_body = 0.0
    for st, ct in zip(fish_stats[1:], fish_centers[1:]):
        # Width-to-height between one and three gives elongated bodies credit without rewarding narrow grass lines.
        aspect = st[cv2.CC_STAT_WIDTH] / max(st[cv2.CC_STAT_HEIGHT], 1)
        # Occupancy rejects disconnected-looking, branching vegetation silhouettes inside a component's bounding box.
        fill = st[cv2.CC_STAT_AREA] / max(st[cv2.CC_STAT_WIDTH] * st[cv2.CC_STAT_HEIGHT], 1)
        # A visibly broad horizontal shape near the image centre is more plausible than a tiny edge fragment.
        extent = min(st[cv2.CC_STAT_AREA] / (160 ** 2 * .10), 1.0)
        # The centre distance has one image-width scale, so composition is only weak evidence.
        proximity = max(0.0, 1.0 - np.hypot(ct[0] / 160 - .5, ct[1] / 160 - .5))
        # All multipliers are bounded semantic votes; axis ratios 1 and 3 describe round and very elongated shapes.
        fish_body = max(fish_body, extent * fill * proximity * max(0.0, min(aspect - 1, 1)) * max(0.0, min(3 - aspect, 1)))
    # Canny hysteresis thresholds mark moderate visible boundaries on the standard 8-bit intensity scale.
    edges = cv2.Canny(np.uint8(v * 255), 50, 100)
    # The guide bar is at least one sixth image-width long, with gaps allowed over teeth and logos.
    lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(edges, 1, np.pi / 180, 20, minLineLength=25, maxLineGap=8)
    blade = 0.0
    if lines is not None:
        # Limit to the first eighty strongest enumerated lines to bound quadratic pair work, without choosing class-specific lines.
        q = lines.reshape(-1, 4)[:80].astype(np.float32)
        # Segment centres, lengths and unit axes permit an analytic parallel-strip test.
        delta = q[:, 2:] - q[:, :2]
        length = np.sqrt(np.sum(delta ** 2, axis=1))
        axis = delta / np.maximum(length[:, None], 1)
        mid = (q[:, :2] + q[:, 2:]) / 2
        # Absolute dot products identify parallel edges regardless of which endpoint Hough lists first.
        parallel = np.abs(axis @ axis.T) > np.cos(np.pi / 18)
        # Project centre differences across and along each candidate's direction to estimate bar thickness and overlap.
        diff = mid[:, None, :] - mid[None, :, :]
        across = np.abs(diff[:, :, 0] * axis[:, None, 1] - diff[:, :, 1] * axis[:, None, 0])
        along = np.abs(np.sum(diff * axis[:, None, :], axis=2))
        # A bar has distinct edges two to sixteen pixels apart and an overlap exceeding half the shorter edge.
        valid = parallel & (across > 2) & (across < 16) & (along < np.minimum(length[:, None], length[None, :]) / 2)
        # Neutral interior is sampled at the middle between each edge pair; chromatic objects are less plausible steel.
        between = np.clip(((mid[:, None, :] + mid[None, :, :]) / 2).astype(int), 0, 159)
        neutral = chroma[between[:, :, 1], between[:, :, 0]] < .16
        # A guide bar should be at least four times as long as thick; image-fraction length is the bounded vote.
        slender = np.minimum(length[:, None], length[None, :]) > across * 4
        # Forty pixels is one quarter of image width, a visibly substantial guide bar rather than a switch or cable.
        blade = float(np.max(np.minimum(length[:, None], length[None, :]) * valid * neutral * slender) / 160)
    # All colour fractions share the same broad centre preference and are bounded quantities with direct interpretations.
    den = float(center.sum())
    return dict(white=float(np.sum(white * center) / den), brown=float(np.sum(brown * center) / den),
                dark=float(np.sum(dark * center) / den), olive=float(np.sum(olive * center) / den),
                green=float(np.mean(green)), orange=float(np.sum(orange * center) / den),
                coat_adjacency=coat_adjacency, coat_texture=coat_texture, olive_fine=olive_fine,
                horizontal_boundary=horizontal_boundary, orange_blob=orange_blob, fish_body=fish_body, blade=blade)


def organic_scores(rgb):
    f = organic_features(rgb)
    # Scores are semantic evidence counts: paired fur colours matter jointly; fractions are rescaled to visible patch sizes.
    dog = min(f['white'] / .20, 1.0) * min((f['brown'] + f['dark']) / .20, 1.0)
    # Adjacent coat patches and mesoscopic texture reinforce the dog interpretation; factors merely match unit-sized votes.
    dog += min(f['coat_adjacency'] / .04, 1.0) + min(f['coat_texture'] / .04, 1.0)
    # Olive is fish-like when it is substantial and fine texture is modest; arbitrary small patches alone are weak evidence.
    fish = min(f['olive'] / .30, 1.0) + max(0.0, 1.0 - f['olive_fine'] / .04)
    # Horizontal olive boundaries support an elongated fish silhouette; foliage does not get this geometric bonus by itself.
    fish += max(0.0, (f['horizontal_boundary'] - .5) * 2)
    # A coherent orange housing is a strong chainsaw cue; fragmented colour evidence receives a weaker independent vote.
    saw = min(f['orange_blob'] / .04, 1.0) * 2 + min(f['orange'] / .12, 1.0)
    return dict(tench=fish, english_springer=dog, chain_saw=saw)

"""Hand-designed long-edge and spatial-layout evidence for manufactured objects."""
import cv2
import numpy as np


def geometry_features(rgb):
    # A 128 square permits inexpensive object-scale morphology with the same coordinate system for each class.
    a = cv2.resize(rgb, (128, 128), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    # Averaging primaries measures neutral structural brightness without assuming a class-specific colour.
    g = a.astype(np.float32).mean(axis=2)
    # Sobel derivatives find object boundaries; dividing by eight normalizes this standard stencil's positive mass.
    gx = cv2.Sobel(g, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3) / 8
    # The perpendicular derivative supplies horizontal boundaries with the same physical brightness units.
    gy = cv2.Sobel(g, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3) / 8
    # Ten byte-scale brightness levels retain visible structural boundaries while rejecting JPEG fluctuations.
    edge = (np.hypot(gx, gy) > 10).astype(np.uint8)
    # A 2:1 direction ratio tolerates mild perspective but excludes roof diagonals and curved organic boundaries.
    he = ((np.abs(gy) > 2 * np.abs(gx)) & (edge > 0)).astype(np.uint8)
    # Transposing the criterion isolates upright walls and machine cabinet sides.
    ve = ((np.abs(gx) > 2 * np.abs(gy)) & (edge > 0)).astype(np.uint8)
    # Three-pixel closing repairs little gaps along a physical edge without merging separate objects.
    hc = cv2.morphologyEx(he, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((1, 3), np.uint8))
    # The vertical analogue repairs upright edges.
    vc = cv2.morphologyEx(ve, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((3, 1), np.uint8))
    # Twelve pixels is about a tenth-frame straight run, longer than most individual leaf or fur edges.
    hl = cv2.morphologyEx(hc, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((1, 12), np.uint8))
    # Upright straight runs indicate pumps and facades, while decks and trucks favor horizontal runs.
    vl = cv2.morphologyEx(vc, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((12, 1), np.uint8))
    # A one-count denominator guard makes the fraction well-defined on an entirely blank photograph.
    line = float((hl.sum() + vl.sum()) / (edge.sum() + 1))
    # Axis alignment is a looser manufactured-object cue than long-edge support.
    axis = float((he.sum() + ve.sum()) / (edge.sum() + 1))
    # Channel spread below one eighth of the byte range allows ordinary casts on neutral audio cabinets.
    neutral = a.max(axis=2).astype(float) - a.min(axis=2).astype(float) < 32
    # Dark neutral material below one third brightness represents black audio panels rather than green foliage.
    dark = (g < 85) & neutral
    # The middle half-frame emphasizes the object panel over backgrounds.
    darkcentre = float(dark[32:96, 32:96].mean())
    # Half-frame edge-density contrast detects blank sky above a detailed church facade.
    lowerdetail = float(edge[64:].mean() - edge[:64].mean())
    # Church facades usually put both horizontal and vertical structural boundaries below the sky.
    lowerlines = float((hl[64:].mean() + vl[64:].mean()) - (hl[:64].mean() + vl[:64].mean()))
    # A truck's upper cabin sides and lower chassis give opposite changes of vertical and horizontal support.
    trucklayout = float((hl[64:].mean() - hl[:64].mean()) + (vl[:64].mean() - vl[64:].mean()))
    # Absolute occupancies distinguish genuinely long cabinet edges from a few isolated lines in a simple background.
    return dict(line=line, axis=axis, hline=float(hl.mean()), vline=float(vl.mean()),
                darkcentre=darkcentre, lowerdetail=lowerdetail, lowerlines=lowerlines,
                trucklayout=trucklayout)


def geometry_scores(f):
    # Saturation at zero and one lets several independently visible properties contribute comparable evidence.
    def bound(x):
        # Unit clipping limits every geometric cue to one evidence vote.
        return float(np.clip(x, 0, 1))
    # A tenth of the image covered by long upright edges is strong cabinet evidence; this is a chosen occupancy meaning.
    upright = bound(f['vline'] / .1)
    # The same tenth-frame occupancy means strong horizontal cabinet or chassis evidence.
    horizontal = bound(f['hline'] / .1)
    # Half of all visible boundaries forming long straight runs means strongly rectilinear manufactured structure.
    structure = bound(f['line'] / .5)
    # A quarter-frame increase in lower texture means considerable sky-to-facade transition.
    facade = bound(f['lowerdetail'] / .25)
    # A tenth-frame opposite movement of horizontal/vertical support describes the truck cab/chassis arrangement.
    chassis = bound(f['trucklayout'] / .1)
    # A quarter of the central panel being black neutral material is strong audio faceplate evidence.
    panel = bound(f['darkcentre'] / .25)
    # Three evidence votes per class balance independent structure, orientation, and layout; each is a semantic property.
    return dict(cassette_player=structure + horizontal + panel - facade,
                gas_pump=structure + upright + min(horizontal, upright),
                church=facade + bound(f['lowerlines'] / .1) + upright,
                garbage_truck=horizontal + chassis + structure)

"""Hand-designed colour, contour and texture evidence for rounded objects and sky."""
import numpy as np
import cv2
# One OpenCV worker avoids threading overhead on small thumbnails.
cv2.setNumThreads(1)


def round_features(rgb):
    # Work in unit RGB so brightness thresholds express fractions of the display range.
    a = rgb.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    r, g, b = a.transpose(2, 0, 1)
    # Arithmetic luminance treats all channels alike: no coefficients are learned.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # Channel spread separates neutral white golf balls from coloured grass and brass.
    spread = a.max(axis=2) - a.min(axis=2)
    # A five-pixel neighbourhood measures small texture without following individual pixels.
    local = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (0, 0), 1.0)
    # Fine residual detects golf dimples and brass tube boundaries at this thumbnail scale.
    fine = np.abs(gray - local)
    # Sky blue has more blue than red and is bright; 0.04 allows haze while requiring colour.
    blue = (b > r + 0.04) & (b > g - 0.03) & (b > 0.35)
    # Broad smoothness distinguishes sky from blue lettering, machinery and shaded foliage.
    broad = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (0, 0), 3.0)
    # A variation under one twentieth of the range describes a largely smooth sky patch.
    smooth = np.abs(gray - broad) < 0.05
    # Brass reflects warm yellow light: red and green exceed blue, unlike neutral metal.
    gold = (r > b + 0.12) & (g > b + 0.06) & (r > g - 0.03) & (g > 0.22)
    # White ball material can be gray in shadow; allow a fifth of the range in channel spread.
    white = (gray > 0.55) & (spread < 0.20)
    # Green grass supplies context for golf balls, with modest channel gaps to tolerate shadow.
    green = (g > r + 0.03) & (g > b + 0.03)
    # Sky and gold fractions are area-normalised and remain meaningful across image sizes.
    f = {'blue': float(blue.mean()), 'sky': float((blue & smooth).mean()), 'gold': float(gold.mean()), 'green': float(green.mean()), 'white': float(white.mean())}
    # Top-half smooth blue gives evidence for an aerial scene while retaining ground context.
    f['sky_top'] = float((blue & smooth)[:rgb.shape[0] // 2].mean())
    # Sky in the lower half distinguishes airborne canopies from buildings above a ground plane.
    f['sky_bottom'] = float((blue & smooth)[rgb.shape[0] // 2:].mean())
    # Gold edge density measures fine tube structure rather than simply a large yellow wall.
    f['gold_detail'] = float((gold * np.minimum(fine / 0.10, 1.0)).mean())
    # Dimple residual within white material can corroborate a ball without requiring text.
    f['white_detail'] = float((white * np.minimum(fine / 0.05, 1.0)).mean())
    # Closing a three-pixel gap joins dimples inside a ball while preserving its outer contour.
    wm = cv2.morphologyEx(white.astype(np.uint8), cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((3, 3), np.uint8))
    # Connected contours let each image supply its own candidate objects; no exemplars are used.
    contours, _ = cv2.findContours(wm, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL, cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
    ball = 0.0
    ball_area = 0.0
    for contour in contours:
        # Contour area and perimeter express the basic roundness identity 4*pi*A/P^2.
        area = cv2.contourArea(contour)
        perimeter = cv2.arcLength(contour, True)
        # Ignore components below one thousandth of the thumbnail, mostly compression specks.
        if area < rgb.shape[0] * rgb.shape[1] / 1000.0 or perimeter == 0:
            continue
        x, y, w, h = cv2.boundingRect(contour)
        # Round projected balls have comparable width and height; elongated clouds score less.
        aspect = min(w, h) / max(w, h)
        # The circle formula is geometric, and clipping avoids discretisation overshoot.
        # Enclosing-circle fill tolerates textured boundaries better than perimeter-based compactness.
        (_, _), radius = cv2.minEnclosingCircle(contour)
        circular = min(1.0, area / (np.pi * radius * radius))
        # Huge bright backgrounds are not individual balls; require under half the image.
        fraction = area / (rgb.shape[0] * rgb.shape[1])
        # A hand-chosen square-root size factor allows small balls but favours a resolved object.
        size = min(1.0, np.sqrt(fraction / 0.03))
        # Boundary-touching backgrounds are less convincing than closed white object contours.
        interior = 1.0 if x > 0 and y > 0 and x + w < rgb.shape[1] and y + h < rgb.shape[0] else 0.4
        # Roundness, isotropy and size are all necessary, so combine them multiplicatively.
        value = circular * aspect * size * interior if fraction < 0.5 else 0.0
        if value > ball:
            ball, ball_area = float(value), float(fraction)
    f['ball'] = ball
    f['ball_area'] = ball_area
    return f
"""Circle-boundary evidence for a bright ball, designed without examples or fitted values."""
import numpy as np
import cv2


def golf_circle(rgb):
    # Unit RGB and arithmetic brightness avoid any trained colour transform.
    a = rgb.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    # Neutral brightness is the material cue; circular boundaries are checked separately.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # A three-pixel median removes isolated texture specks while retaining the outline.
    mono = cv2.medianBlur(np.uint8(gray * 255.0), 3)
    # A 160-pixel thumbnail resolves radii from five to sixty-five; visible edges use Canny 80.
    # Accumulator 25 asks for a substantial arc, and eight-pixel spacing limits duplicates.
    circles = cv2.HoughCircles(mono, cv2.HOUGH_GRADIENT, 1.0, 8.0, param1=80, param2=25, minRadius=5, maxRadius=65)
    if circles is None:
        return 0.0
    # Twelve strongest hypotheses bound time independently of texture complexity.
    c = circles[0, :12]
    # Twenty-four equally spaced spokes give broad angular support without per-pixel loops.
    angle = np.arange(24) * (2.0 * np.pi / 24.0)
    # Sample three quarters and one and one quarter radii to compare ball surface with background.
    vx, vy = np.cos(angle)[None, :], np.sin(angle)[None, :]
    # Vectorised coordinates collect every circle and spoke in the same interpolation pass.
    xi = c[:, 0, None] + 0.75 * c[:, 2, None] * vx
    yi = c[:, 1, None] + 0.75 * c[:, 2, None] * vy
    # The outer samples must remain outside the bright object's boundary.
    xo = c[:, 0, None] + 1.25 * c[:, 2, None] * vx
    yo = c[:, 1, None] + 1.25 * c[:, 2, None] * vy
    # Linear interpolation avoids dependence on integer alignment of a circular rim.
    inner = cv2.remap(a, xi.astype(np.float32), yi.astype(np.float32), cv2.INTER_LINEAR, borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REPLICATE)
    # All outer RGB samples share one interpolation pass.
    outer = cv2.remap(a, xo.astype(np.float32), yo.astype(np.float32), cv2.INTER_LINEAR, borderMode=cv2.BORDER_REPLICATE)
    # Bright neutral spokes contrast with darker surround; a tenth-range gap is substantial.
    neutral = (inner.max(axis=2) - inner.min(axis=2) < 0.2) & (inner.mean(axis=2) > 0.55)
    # Angular consistency rejects isolated lettering, windows and arbitrary Hough false circles.
    rim = inner.mean(axis=2) > outer.mean(axis=2) + 0.1
    # Three quarters of the spokes must support both neutral surface and bright convex outline.
    support = (neutral & rim).mean(axis=1)
    # Evidence begins only after a half-circle is supported, then rises to complete support.
    evidence = np.clip((support - 0.5) / 0.5, 0.0, 1.0)
    # A ten-pixel radius is comfortably resolved; smaller circles receive proportionate credit.
    evidence *= np.minimum(1.0, c[:, 2] / 10.0)
    return float(evidence.max())

# teacher: a small CNN trained on the 505 training images

A 5-block convolutional network (981,802 parameters) trained from scratch on the 505 images in
`workspace/data/train` and nothing else. It is delivered as numpy weights (`cnn_505.npz`, ~3.9 MB)
plus a numpy-only forward pass (`teacher.py`); no torch is needed.

## How it was trained and how it scores
- Recipe (baseline/cnn_small.py, seed 0): AdamW lr 2e-3 wd 0.05, one-cycle schedule, label smoothing 0.1,
  batch 64, 40 epochs, 128 px, random crop from a 144 px resize + flip + brightness/contrast/saturation jitter.
  The final-epoch weights are used (no early stopping or model selection).
- Accuracy: 99.0% on its 505 training images, 68.1% on the 495 validation images, 68.9% on the hidden test set.
  It memorises the training set, so activations on train images look cleaner than they will on unseen images.

## Classes (logit index order)
0 tench, 1 english_springer, 2 cassette_player, 3 chain_saw, 4 church, 5 french_horn, 6 garbage_truck, 7 gas_pump, 8 golf_ball, 9 parachute

## Preprocessing (identical to the training-time eval transform)
RGB; resize shortest side to 144 (PIL bilinear, other side `round(w*s)`); centre crop 128x128;
divide by 255; subtract mean (0.485, 0.456, 0.406) and divide by std (0.229, 0.224, 0.225) per channel; CHW.

## Layers (output shapes for a 128 px input)
| name | operation | output |
|---|---|---|
| conv1 | conv3x3 3->32 (pad 1, no bias) + BN (eps 1e-5) + ReLU | 32x128x128 |
| pool1 | maxpool 2x2 | 32x64x64 |
| conv2 | conv3x3 32->64 + BN + ReLU | 64x64x64 |
| pool2 | maxpool 2x2 | 64x32x32 |
| conv3 | conv3x3 64->128 + BN + ReLU | 128x32x32 |
| pool3 | maxpool 2x2 | 128x16x16 |
| conv4 | conv3x3 128->256 + BN + ReLU | 256x16x16 |
| pool4 | maxpool 2x2 | 256x8x8 |
| conv5 | conv3x3 256->256 + BN + ReLU | 256x8x8 |
| pool5 | maxpool 2x2 | 256x4x4 |
| gap | global average pool | 256 |
| fc | linear 256->10 (logits) | 10 |
| probs | softmax | 10 |

`conv1..conv5` activations are post BN+ReLU. Weights: `features.N.*` (N = index in the 20-layer feature stack:
conv at 0,4,8,12,16; BN at 1,5,9,13,17) and `fc.weight`/`fc.bias`. Full details are in `arch.json`.

## Using it
From `workspace/`:

    import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "teacher"); import teacher
    m = teacher.load()
    m.layers()                                    # [(name, kind, output_shape), ...]
    logits = m.forward("data/train/church/x.JPEG")                 # (10,)
    logits, acts = m.forward(path, return_activations=True)        # acts: ordered dict name -> array
    cls, probs = m.predict(path)
    m.weights("conv2")                            # dict of that layer's parameter arrays

`forward` also accepts an RGB uint8 HxWx3 array (same resize/crop pipeline; pass `already_cropped=True` to skip it).
About 0.15 s per image on CPU.

Command line (from `workspace/`):

    python3 teacher/teacher.py layers
    python3 teacher/teacher.py predict IMG [IMG ...]
    python3 teacher/teacher.py activations IMG --layer conv3 [--top-channels 10] [--out maps.npz]
    python3 teacher/teacher.py weights --layer conv1 [--out w.npz]
    python3 teacher/teacher.py top --layer conv3 --channel 5 [--k 10]

`top` ranks the training images by a channel's maximum activation (per-layer cache in `teacher/.cache/`,
built on first use, about a minute). The teacher refuses image paths under `data/val`.

"""Analytic straight structure and upright-cabinet/chassis arrangements; no learned parameters."""
import cv2
import numpy as np


def geometry_features(rgb):
    # A 128-pixel square supports object-scale line and cabinet analysis at little cost.
    a = cv2.resize(rgb, (128, 128), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA)
    # Unit RGB gives brightness and colour tolerances a direct fraction-of-range meaning.
    af = a.astype(np.float32) / 255.0
    # Equal-channel brightness avoids colour-specific gradient emphasis for grayscale machinery.
    gray = af.mean(axis=2)
    # The analytic Sobel stencil averages across the edge; eight is its absolute coefficient mass.
    gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3) / 8
    # The perpendicular gradient measures horizontal boundaries in the same intensity units.
    gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3) / 8
    # A twentieth-range local difference is a visible edge rather than small JPEG fluctuations.
    edge = np.hypot(gx, gy) > .05
    # Twice the competing derivative allows about a quarter-turn's third of perspective tolerance.
    he = ((np.abs(gy) > 2 * np.abs(gx)) & edge).astype(np.uint8)
    # The transposed criterion isolates upright walls, display sides and cabinet uprights.
    ve = ((np.abs(gx) > 2 * np.abs(gy)) & edge).astype(np.uint8)
    # Closing three-pixel holes repairs little interruptions in the same straight physical boundary.
    hc = cv2.morphologyEx(he, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((1, 3), np.uint8))
    # The same operation along columns repairs vertical edges.
    vc = cv2.morphologyEx(ve, cv2.MORPH_CLOSE, np.ones((3, 1), np.uint8))
    # A tenth-frame straight run is substantial machine/building structure, longer than individual fur edges.
    hl = cv2.morphologyEx(hc, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((1, 12), np.uint8))
    # Vertical runs use the same physical minimum length.
    vl = cv2.morphologyEx(vc, cv2.MORPH_OPEN, np.ones((12, 1), np.uint8))
    # A tiny denominator guard handles blank photographs without adding meaningful evidence.
    den = float(edge.sum()) + 1e-6
    # Manufactured objects concentrate boundaries along axes and into coherent straight runs.
    f = dict(axis=float((he.sum()+ve.sum())/den), line=float((hl.sum()+vl.sum())/den),
             hline=float(hl.mean()), vline=float(vl.mean()))
    # Relative line orientation separates broad decks/truck bodies from tall dispenser cabinets.
    f['upright'] = float(vl.sum() / (vl.sum()+hl.sum()+1e-6))
    # Row coordinates are dimensionless fractions, so a displacement can mean a fraction of image height.
    y = np.arange(128, dtype=np.float32)[:,None] / 128
    # Horizontal chassis edges tend to lie below upright cabin edges, unlike uniform audio faceplates.
    hy = float((hl*y).sum() / (hl.sum()+1e-6))
    # The vertical-edge centroid locates upright cab, pump and wall structure.
    vy = float((vl*y).sum() / (vl.sum()+1e-6))
    # This signed difference isolates cab-above-chassis layout independent of total boundary strength.
    f['chassis_offset'] = hy-vy
    # Sky-to-facade transition raises lower-half detail in church views; half-frame split is geometric.
    f['lowerdetail'] = float(edge[64:].mean()-edge[:64].mean())
    # Lower straight structure helps reject upper trees as the cause of the detail transition.
    f['lowerlines'] = float(hl[64:].mean()+vl[64:].mean()-hl[:64].mean()-vl[:64].mean())
    # Neutral material permits mild colour cast, while one-third brightness describes a dark audio panel.
    neutral = af.max(axis=2)-af.min(axis=2) < 1/8
    # Dark central material is common to black/silver audio decks but is not independently enough to classify them.
    dark = (gray < 1/3) & neutral
    # The central half-frame suppresses bright photographic borders around a player.
    f['darkcentre'] = float(dark[32:96,32:96].mean())
    # Standard Canny thresholds at one fifth and two fifths byte-range isolate substantial cabinet outlines.
    edges = cv2.Canny(np.uint8(gray*255), 50, 100)
    # Hough segments a fifth-frame long, with small gaps, are possible upright cabinet edges.
    lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(edges, 1, np.pi/180, 20, minLineLength=25, maxLineGap=5)
    f['cabinet'] = 0.0
    f['display'] = 0.0
    if lines is None:
        return f
    # At most eighty returned edges bound the pairwise geometric work even in detailed facades.
    q = lines.reshape(-1,4)[:80].astype(np.float32)
    # Limit slope to one horizontal step per three vertical steps, allowing perspective on an upright pump.
    upright = np.abs(q[:,2]-q[:,0])*3 < np.abs(q[:,3]-q[:,1])
    q = q[upright]
    if len(q) < 2:
        return f
    # Each upright is represented by its mean horizontal position and vertical extent.
    x = (q[:,0]+q[:,2])/2
    # Sorting the endpoint heights makes segment order irrelevant.
    top, bottom = np.minimum(q[:,1],q[:,3]), np.maximum(q[:,1],q[:,3])
    # Pairs of upright sides imply a common rectangle only where their heights overlap.
    x0, x1 = np.minimum(x[:,None],x[None,:]), np.maximum(x[:,None],x[None,:])
    # The overlap excludes mismatched unrelated edges at distant heights.
    y0, y1 = np.maximum(top[:,None],top[None,:]), np.minimum(bottom[:,None],bottom[None,:])
    # Broad upright cabinets are at least an eighth-frame wide and a quarter-frame tall.
    width, height = x1-x0, y1-y0
    # A height comparable to width rejects short horizontal tape-player panels.
    valid = (width>16)&(width<80)&(height>32)&(height>width*.8)
    # Half-frame overlap counts as a full cabinet-side vote; shorter visible cabinets get partial credit.
    extent = np.minimum(np.maximum(height,0)/64,1)
    # Different edge lengths get credit in proportion to their common supported fraction.
    alignment = np.maximum(height,0)/np.maximum(np.minimum((bottom-top)[:,None],(bottom-top)[None,:]),1)
    # Compact upright rectangle support is bounded and does not prefer a specific training image size.
    quality = valid*extent*alignment
    f['cabinet'] = float(quality.max()) if quality.size else 0.0
    # White/coloured panels with an upper dark display are a semantic pump arrangement.
    ii = cv2.integral(dark.astype(np.float32))
    # Rectangle integration measures all candidate displays without per-pixel loops.
    def rectangles(left,right,upper,lower):
        # Clip every bound to the fixed thumbnail extent and keep integer area nonzero.
        l,r = np.clip(left.astype(int),0,127),np.clip(right.astype(int),1,128)
        # The vertical counterpart gives valid integral-image bounds at cropped cabinets.
        t,b = np.clip(upper.astype(int),0,127),np.clip(lower.astype(int),1,128)
        # Four-corner inclusion/exclusion is exact rectangular dark-material occupancy.
        return (ii[b,r]-ii[t,r]-ii[b,l]+ii[t,l])/np.maximum((r-l)*(b-t),1)
    # The central half-width avoids dark cabinet sides and hose hardware.
    left,right = x0+width/4,x1-width/4
    # A display usually occupies the upper-middle third rather than the plinth or the top sign.
    updark = rectangles(left,right,y0+height/6,y0+height/2)
    # The lower half should have less dark neutral area than the digital-display region.
    lowdark = rectangles(left,right,y0+height/2,y1-height/8)
    # A quarter-range occupancy increase is a clear small upper screen over a painted lower body.
    contrast = np.clip((updark-lowdark)/.25,0,1)
    # Cabinet geometry gates display evidence so random dark patches on dogs/foliage cannot count.
    f['display'] = float((quality*contrast).max()) if quality.size else 0.0
    return f


def geometry_scores(f):
    # Unit clipping makes semantic cues comparable without fitting score coefficients.
    def bound(x):
        # Each cue gets at most one independent evidence vote.
        return float(np.clip(x, 0, 1))
    # A tenth-frame straight-edge occupancy is a clearly resolved horizontal machine structure.
    horizontal = bound(f['hline']/.1)
    # Upright occupancy uses the same visual scale for dispensers and facades.
    vertical = bound(f['vline']/.1)
    # A quarter of the central crop as dark neutral material is a substantial audio faceplate.
    panel = bound(f['darkcentre']/.25)
    # A quarter-frame increase in lower detail is a strong sky-to-building transition.
    facade = bound(f['lowerdetail']/.25)
    # A tenth-frame increase in lower straight edges corroborates actual architecture rather than foliage.
    lowerstructure = bound(f['lowerlines']/.1)
    # A quarter-frame downward displacement of horizontal versus vertical structure is a clear chassis layout.
    chassis = bound(f['chassis_offset']/.25)
    # Two independent axle/body layout votes favour trucks; display and cabinet each add a pump vote.
    return dict(cassette_player=horizontal+panel+(1-f['upright'])-facade,
                gas_pump=vertical+f['cabinet']+f['display'],
                church=facade+lowerstructure+f['upright'],
                garbage_truck=horizontal+2*chassis+(1-f['upright']))

# Geometry v2 train-only investigation

Scope: train only, no viewer, no validation, no fitted values, no other agents. Existing teacher first-layer and intervention inspection was read first; new teacher interventions are in geometry_teacher_v2.py/log. New independently specified analytic features are in geometry_v2.py; no teacher values enter that file.

## Teacher mechanism and consequence

The CNN preserves most machine labels under grayscale but loses them under large blur and quarter-turn. New interventions use the same square-resized original as the control and compare vertical flip, quadrant permutation and blur along a single image axis. We read mean conv3 and conv5 activation to establish that local activity can remain while output changes; those values are diagnostic only.

Of three sampled cassettes, two controls were correct after square-resizing (the other became truck), and all three vertical flips were classified cassette. Two of three quadrant permutations lost cassette. Of three church controls all were correct, two vertical flips and two quadrant permutations lost church. Of three truck controls all correct, all three vertical flips lost truck, two quadrant permutations lost truck. Of three pump controls all correct, all three vertical flips retained pump, two quadrant permutations lost pump. Axis-specific blurs selectively damaged these classes, consistent with object layout and orientation of boundaries. This motivates retaining horizontal/vertical structure and its spatial arrangement rather than merely counting all edges.

## Own pixel measurements before rules

All 505 training images processed by geometry_spatial.py and geometry_stats.py. Existing feature medians: long-line support cassette .474, pump .443, truck .355, church .290; organic classes approximately .19-.28. Near-axis boundary fraction cassette .792, pump .790, truck .754, church .701; organic classes .64-.68. Median lower-minus-upper half edge density church .174, every other class -.045 to +.014. Median horizontal-edge y centroid minus vertical-edge y centroid truck +.139, church +.058, cassette -.034, pump -.060. These are explanatory summaries only; they are not arrays/constants in classifier code.

Hough roof probe failed: at a chosen eighth-frame roof-support trigger, church 41/55 fired but dog 42/50, horn44/50 and tench42/50 also fired. Sloping edge pairs are generic at this scale. No roof rule added.

## New features

geometry_v2.py recomputes axis and long-line support at an independently chosen .05 brightness derivative threshold, then adds normalized horizontal-minus-vertical line centroids, upright relative line mass, and upright Hough edge-pair cabinets. The cabinet candidate has at least eighth-frame width and quarter-frame overlap, and the upper-screen feature tests a dark upper-middle panel against a less dark lower body. Every scale represents a named geometric fraction or visible brightness fraction. The file is commented line by line.

All-train trigger counts from geometry_v2_analysis.py:

| Feature trigger | Cassette | Saw | Church | Dog | Horn | Truck | Pump | Golf | Para | Tench |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| chassis offset >1/8 height |6|20|17|11|14|25|4|11|20|18|
| cabinet >.75 unit support |12|15|17|10|11|8|24|8|5|15|
| upper display >.5 support |8|8|18|9|6|4|19|4|0|6|
| lower detail increase >1/8 |7|3|30|7|9|6|3|5|4|1|

Conclusion: cabinet/display and chassis should be context-gated, not independent hard decisions. Lower detail remains the most selective church evidence. A few unsupported Hough edges in a smooth sky can yield a large centroid offset, so chassis should require substantial line occupancy. Upright relative mass separates pumps from cassette, but churches also have strong upright edges.

## Rule trial and causal ablation

One deliberately specified four-way semantic vote trial was measured over only the four relevant class folders (205 images), without threshold search. Old geometry_scores from geometry_features.py gives95/205=46.34%; new geometry_scores gives96/205=46.83%, which is no meaningful improvement. Per-class old -> new: cassette31/50 ->27/50, pump26/50 ->21/50, church28/55 ->22/55, truck10/50 ->26/50.

Within the new formula, ablating only display and chassis-offset gives84/205=40.98% (cassette37, pump14, church33, truck0). Reintroducing the features fixes26 trucks and8 pumps, breaks10 cassettes,11 churches and1 pump: net+12 images. Thus these features do causally alter relevant images but need gating. Do not replace main classifier wholesale with these four-way scores. Useful contribution is the bounded normalized chassis feature, cabinet/display as weak corroboration, and lower-detail church feature.

## Negative alternative: circular tyre templates

A genuinely different radial dark-ring template bank was tested in tyre_probe.py. Five hand-chosen radii span4..18 pixels; each candidate is a neutral dark annulus against a brighter surrounding annulus, and pairs must align horizontally in the lower half. All505 train images processed. It did NOT separate wheels: median pair response truck .682, cassette .656, church .619, dog .601, tench .593. At a chosen .25 response threshold, truck49/50 fire but tench49/50, church53/55 and most others also fire. Even gated by axis>.75, truck28/50, cassette28/50 and pump35/50 fire. This detector merely finds dark patches; it is not in geometry_v2.py.

No validation measurements were performed. No auto-selection of constants, learned tables, teacher constants, pretrained modules, image viewing or external files were used. Recommended integration is selective use of chassis_offset with line-occupancy gate, and conservative church facade evidence; cabinet and display are optional weak signals.

"""Analytic material and photographic context cues for horn, golf, and parachute."""
import numpy as np
import cv2


def round_v2(rgb):
    # A 160-pixel thumbnail resolves tube detail while keeping each image pass inexpensive.
    a = cv2.resize(rgb, (160, 160), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32) / 255
    # Opponent channels distinguish blue sky, green lawn and yellow metal without learned transforms.
    r, g, b = a.transpose(2, 0, 1)
    # Arithmetic brightness treats primaries alike in texture measurements.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # HSV saturation and maximum brightness describe neutral cloudy sky analytically.
    hsv = cv2.cvtColor(a, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)
    # The two channels permit gray clouds as well as blue sky, without accepting dark neutral machinery.
    saturation, value = hsv[:, :, 1], hsv[:, :, 2]
    # Standard three-tap Sobel gradients estimate boundary strength; four converts the stencil to unit-contrast scale.
    gx = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_32F, 1, 0, ksize=3) / 4
    # The perpendicular derivative uses the same normalization for geometrically meaningful directions.
    gy = cv2.Sobel(gray, cv2.CV_32F, 0, 1, ksize=3) / 4
    # Euclidean magnitude measures boundaries independently of orientation.
    mag = np.hypot(gx, gy)
    # Blue sky visibly exceeds red, tolerates slightly cyan coloration, and is brighter than dark blue paint.
    blue = (b > r + .04) & (b > g - .03) & (b > .35)
    # Cloudy sky is brighter than midgray and has less than fifteen percent HSV saturation.
    cloud = (saturation < .15) & (value > .55)
    # Four percent local brightness change denotes smooth sky rather than grass, fur or textured machinery.
    sky = (blue | cloud) & (mag < .04)
    # Brass is yellow and bright: the green/red ratio permits warm gold while excluding dark red-brown fur.
    gold = (r > b + .12) & (g > b + .06) & (g > .40) & (g > r * .70) & (g < r * 1.05)
    # A tenth-range gradient is a substantial tube or object boundary, rather than minor surface shading.
    edge = mag > .10
    # About fifteen degrees around image axes identify straight panels/facades rather than broadly curved tubing.
    axis = np.minimum(np.abs(gx), np.abs(gy)) < .27 * np.maximum(np.abs(gx), np.abs(gy))
    # One-pixel residual responds to closely spaced brass highlights and tube edges.
    fine = np.abs(gray - cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (0, 0), 1))
    # Side strips each one eighth frame wide test whether sky surrounds the object, unlike sky only above a church.
    border = np.concatenate((sky[:, :20].ravel(), sky[:, -20:].ravel()))
    # Grass has a visible green excess over both other primaries; modest gaps tolerate shadow and atmospheric casts.
    green = (g > r + .03) & (g > b + .03)
    # A white ball can be gray in shade; a fifth-range channel spread admits mild blue shadows.
    white = (gray > .5) & (np.ptp(a, axis=2) < .2)
    # Conditional averages describe material texture independently of how much material is present; a one-pixel guard handles empty masks.
    gold_count = max(int(gold.sum()), 1)
    # Half-image lower sky and side sky capture aerial context; bright-gold details describe metal, smooth green describes blurred lawn.
    return dict(sky_all=float(sky.mean()), sky_lower=float(sky[80:].mean()), sky_border=float(border.mean()),
                blue_lower=float((blue & (mag < .04))[80:].mean()),
                bright_gold=float(gold.mean()), curved_gold=float((gold & edge & ~axis).mean()),
                axis_gold=float((gold & edge & axis).mean()),
                detailed_gold=float((gold * fine).mean()), gold_fine=float((gold * fine).sum() / gold_count),
                smooth_green=float((green & (mag < .05)).mean()),
                edge_fraction=float(edge.mean()), white_fraction=float(white.mean()))


def context_triggers(f):
    # A fifth-frame smooth lawn, sparse visible edges and some white material form a strong golf photographic-context cue.
    golf = f['smooth_green'] > .20 and f['edge_fraction'] < .20 and f['white_fraction'] > .02
    # Sky filling most lower side context supports a canopy suspended in air; white studio backdrops remain a known ambiguity.
    parachute = f['sky_lower'] > .40 and f['sky_border'] > .50
    # Resolved warm tube detail means at least one twentieth frame of brass and four percent fine residual within it.
    horn = f['bright_gold'] > .05 and f['gold_fine'] > .04
    return dict(golf_ball=golf, parachute=parachute, french_horn=horn)
# Round/context investigation v2 (train only)

No validation access. Teacher weights inspected first with `teacher.py weights --layer conv1` and README; no numeric weight/activation copied into classifier code. `round_analysis.py` tested first four sorted train examples of each target class with original, grayscale, global blur. All four horns fail after sigma-three blur; all four golf images retain golf decisions and three increase target margin after blur. Two of four parachutes fail after grayscale, but all survive global blur. Consequence: emphasize resolved warm high-frequency structure for brass; smooth low-frequency photographic context for golf and parachute. No outputs/activations were fit.

`round_causal_v2.py` additionally selectively blurs bright yellow pixels and complementary pixels, and makes blue pixels neutral while preserving their brightness. Warm-only blur reduces the target margin on all four horns (still correctly classified); complementary blur reduces all four too and changes one decision. Neutralizing sky changes two of four parachutes to machines, while none of the four golf images changes class. This supports independent color and fine-boundary mechanisms, not a claim of a specific learned channel meaning.

Implementation: `round_v2.py` contains only independently chosen RGB/HSV material intervals, standard Sobel derivative, one-pixel fine residual, half-image and side-margin pools. Returns semantic features plus optional fixed context triggers. Every feature constant has a visual or geometric explanation. It does not load teacher or any stored statistics. Root should integrate features into its shared passes to avoid duplicate image work.

## Measurements

`round_probe_v2.py`, all 505 train images, diagnostic medians only (not embedded parameter tables): smooth blue-or-gray sky in lower half = parachute .663, cassette .140, pump .122, truck .095, horn .063, dog .058, church .038, saw .037, golf .035, tench .034. It detects arbitrary white patches, not reliably balls.

A shape score>.6 fired only one golf image and no other class; context score>.6 fired no images. Median ball shape golf .042, dog .004, pump .079, tench .056. Too weak to add. """Analytic organic-object arrangements, without learned constants or reference images."""
import numpy as np
import cv2


def _rect_mean(integral, x0, y0, x1, y1, width, height):
    # All candidate windows are evaluated together with the integral-image rectangle identity.
    oh, ow = integral.shape[0] - height, integral.shape[1] - width
    # Division by rectangle area gives a material occupancy independent of candidate size.
    return (integral[y1:y1+oh, x1:x1+ow] - integral[y0:y0+oh, x1:x1+ow] - integral[y1:y1+oh, x0:x0+ow] + integral[y0:y0+oh, x0:x0+ow]) / max((x1-x0)*(y1-y0), 1)


def organic_features_v2(rgb):
    # A 160-square thumbnail allows multiscale head and guide-bar geometry below the latency budget.
    a = cv2.resize(np.asarray(rgb), (160, 160), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32) / 255
    # RGB ordering distinguishes dark warm ears from white fur and orange housings.
    r, g, b = a.transpose(2, 0, 1)
    # Arithmetic brightness and channel spread are analytic material descriptors.
    gray = a.mean(axis=2)
    # Channel spread measures distance from neutral fur or painted white machinery.
    spread = a.max(axis=2)-a.min(axis=2)
    # A half-range white threshold admits fur in shade; one fifth spread excludes coloured ears.
    white = (gray > .5) & (spread < .2)
    # Warm dark patches represent springer ears; small ratios allow gray lighting while retaining warm order.
    brown = (r > g*1.08) & (g > b*1.05) & (gray < .55) & (gray > .08)
    # A dark nose is near the bottom of a typical face; one quarter brightness is visibly dark.
    dark = gray < .25
    # Saturated orange/red is a likely saw housing; it must stand apart from natural warm brown.
    orange = (r > .5) & (r > g+.2) & (g > b+.05) & (b < .35)
    # Summed-area maps permit material arrangement tests without per-pixel Python loops.
    ints = {k: cv2.integral(v.astype(np.float32)) for k,v in [('white',white),('brown',brown),('dark',dark)]}
    face = 0.0
    for size in (40, 64, 96, 128):
        # Four manually chosen head scales cover one quarter through four fifths of image width.
        def rect(material, x0, y0, x1, y1):
            # Rectangle coordinates are fractions of a square dog-head candidate, rounded only for rasterisation.
            q = [int(round(x*size)) for x in (x0,y0,x1,y1)]
            return _rect_mean(ints[material], *q, size, size)
        # Two warm outer lobes are the long ears around a central pale muzzle; tenths give broad regions.
        left = rect('brown', .05, .15, .35, .8)
        # The right region is the mirror image, requiring bilateral rather than incidental brown context.
        right = rect('brown', .65, .15, .95, .8)
        # A white vertical blaze runs down the middle of many springer faces.
        blaze = rect('white', .4, .1, .6, .65)
        # The small dark nose lies below that blaze, centrally between the ears.
        nose = rect('dark', .4, .65, .6, .85)
        # Multiplication requires all parts; square-rooting ear support tolerates an ear partly in shadow.
        value = np.sqrt(left*right) * blaze * nose
        # Max pooling expresses one plausible resolved head anywhere in the image.
        face = max(face, float(value.max()))
    # Moderate Canny thresholds denote object boundaries; small JPEG variation is ignored.
    edges = cv2.Canny(np.uint8(gray*255), 50, 100)
    # Guide-bar boundaries must span about one fifth frame; eight-pixel gaps tolerate logos and chain teeth.
    lines = cv2.HoughLinesP(edges, 1, np.pi/180, 20, minLineLength=30, maxLineGap=8)
    bar_housing = 0.0
    if lines is not None:
        # Eighty candidate edges bound pairwise work in highly textured vegetation.
        q=lines.reshape(-1,4)[:80].astype(np.float32)
        # Segment directions and centres support rotation-independent narrow-bar geometry.
        d=q[:,2:]-q[:,:2]
        length=np.hypot(d[:,0],d[:,1])
        # A unit floor avoids dividing by zero for any degenerate Hough segment.
        axis=d/np.maximum(length[:,None],1)
        # A bar candidate sits midway between a pair of near-parallel outlines.
        mid=(q[:,:2]+q[:,2:])/2
        # Parallelism within ten degrees tolerates perspective, but not crossing roof edges.
        parallel=np.abs(axis@axis.T)>np.cos(np.pi/18)
        # Across/along separations distinguish a narrow strip from unrelated distant parallel lines.
        diff=mid[:,None,:]-mid[None,:,:]
        across=np.abs(diff[:,:,0]*axis[:,None,1]-diff[:,:,1]*axis[:,None,0])
        # Along-axis separation must leave more than half the shorter edge in overlap.
        along=np.abs(np.sum(diff*axis[:,None,:],axis=2))
        # A guide bar is four times longer than thick, two to sixteen pixels wide, and substantially overlaps.
        shorter=np.minimum(length[:,None],length[None,:])
        valid=parallel&(across>2)&(across<16)&(shorter>4*across)&(along<shorter/2)
        # Midpoint material should be neutral steel, allowing one fifth channel spread for reflected light.
        centre=(mid[:,None,:]+mid[None,:,:])/2
        # Raster coordinates are clipped to the thumbnail only for robust border sampling.
        pix=np.clip(centre.astype(int),0,159)
        neutral=spread[pix[:,:,1],pix[:,:,0]]<.2

        sample=centre[None,:,:,:]+np.array([-.3,0,.3],np.float32)[:,None,None,None]*shorter[None,:,:,None]*axis[None,:,None,:]

        normal=np.stack([-axis[:,1],axis[:,0]],axis=1)

        sides=np.stack([sample-.6*across[None,:,:,None]*normal[None,:,None,:],sample+.6*across[None,:,:,None]*normal[None,:,None,:]])

        sp=np.clip(sample.astype(int),0,159)

        steel=((spread[sp[:,:,:,1],sp[:,:,:,0]]<.2)&(gray[sp[:,:,:,1],sp[:,:,:,0]]>.35)).mean(axis=0)

        sd=np.clip(sides.astype(int),0,159)
        # A tenth-range contrast denotes a visible dark chain on lighter metal.
        chain=(gray[sp[:,:,:,1],sp[:,:,:,0]][None,:,:,:]>gray[sd[:,:,:,:,1],sd[:,:,:,:,0]]+.1).mean(axis=(0,1))
        # A broad orange neighbourhood near a bar endpoint represents the attached motor housing.
        housing=cv2.GaussianBlur(orange.astype(np.float32),(0,0),10)
        # One half the shorter edge length locates the candidate's two ends.
        ends=np.stack([centre-shorter[:,:,None]*axis[:,None,:]/2,centre+shorter[:,:,None]*axis[:,None,:]/2])
        # Nearest raster sampling is enough for a ten-pixel-smoothed material map.
        ep=np.clip(ends.astype(int),0,159)
        # Either bar end may attach to the motor; a fifth-image-wide orange patch is meaningful housing support.
        orange_end=np.max(housing[ep[:,:,:,1],ep[:,:,:,0]],axis=0)
        # Orange should belong to the motor at an end, rather than diffuse warm wood or brick behind a neutral line.
        orange_end=np.maximum(orange_end-housing[pix[:,:,1],pix[:,:,0]],0)
        # Length is expressed as frame fraction, and all geometric/material conditions are required together.
        bar_housing=float(np.max(shorter/160*valid*neutral*orange_end*steel*chain))
    return {'dog_face':face,'saw_bar_housing':bar_housing}


def broad_coat_features(rgb):
    # A 160-square thumbnail matches the coat-patch scales to fixed image fractions.
    a = cv2.resize(np.asarray(rgb), (160,160), interpolation=cv2.INTER_AREA).astype(np.float32)/255
    # Brightness and chroma distinguish pale fur from brown ears and black coat patches.
    r,g,b=a.transpose(2,0,1)
    # Equal-channel brightness has no fitted luminance parameters.
    gray=a.mean(axis=2)
    # Primary spread separates white from coloured material without a learned transform.
    spread=a.max(axis=2)-a.min(axis=2)
    # White over half brightness and under roughly one sixth spread includes fur with mild shadow/cast.
    white=(gray>.55)&(spread<.16)
    # Muted warm brown, with visible but not strongly saturated chroma, denotes liver-coloured fur rather than red enamel.
    brown=(r>g*1.10)&(g>b*1.08)&(gray>.08)&(gray<.55)&(spread>.04)&(spread<.35)
    # One fifth brightness represents dark ears/noses or the black half of a black-and-white coat.
    dark=gray<.20
    # Eleven pixels is about seven percent width: genuine coat interiors survive while narrow brass glints disappear.
    broad=cv2.morphologyEx(white.astype(np.uint8),cv2.MORPH_OPEN,cv2.getStructuringElement(cv2.MORPH_ELLIPSE,(11,11)))
    # The same seven-percent neighbourhood checks that the coloured patch actually adjoins pale coat material.
    near=cv2.dilate(broad,np.ones((11,11),np.uint8))>0
    # Central seven tenths discounts border backgrounds without assuming the whole animal fits inside the frame.
    center=np.zeros_like(gray)
    center[24:136,24:136]=1
    # Adjacent fur fractions are expressed over the image, retaining direct visible-area meaning.
    adjacency=float(np.mean((brown|dark)*near*center))
    # The warm-only version is less likely to count the black trim around a white machine cabinet.
    brown_adjacency=float(np.mean(brown*near*center))
    # White-component contours expose curved coat outlines rather than just white panel area.
    contours,_=cv2.findContours(broad,cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL,cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_NONE)
    curved=0.0
    for contour in contours:
        # Components under one percent frame are too small for meaningful coat-shape evidence.
        if cv2.contourArea(contour)<160**2*.01:
            continue
        # Four-pixel contour chords suppress single-pixel staircase artifacts in edge orientation.
        xy=contour[:,0,:].astype(np.float32)
        d=np.roll(xy,-4,axis=0)-xy
        # Arc-length weighting gives broad physical boundaries more influence than dense raster sampling.
        length=np.hypot(d[:,0],d[:,1])
        # Directions more than fifteen degrees from either axis favour curved fur patches over cabinet rectangles.
        nonaxis=np.minimum(abs(d[:,0]),abs(d[:,1]))>.27*np.maximum(abs(d[:,0]),abs(d[:,1]))
        # A one-unit guard handles any degenerate contour without changing ordinary boundary ratios.
        curvy=float(np.sum(length*nonaxis)/(length.sum()+1))
        # Isolate the component interior to assess a seven-percent-width exterior ring.
        cmask=np.zeros_like(broad)
        cv2.drawContours(cmask,[contour],0,1,-1)
        # A local ring asks for brown coat immediately outside the pale patch, rather than unrelated brown elsewhere.
        ring=(cv2.dilate(cmask,np.ones((11,11),np.uint8))>0)&(cmask==0)
        # Brown occupancy is measured in this one image, never learned or stored across images.
        share=float((brown*ring).sum()/(ring.sum()+1))
        # A tenth-frame patch is visibly resolved; smaller patches receive proportionate size credit.
        area=float(np.sum(cmask*center)/160**2)
        # All three necessary properties combine: resolved pale patch, warm fur ring, nonrectangular contour.
        curved=max(curved,min(area/.10,1)*share*curvy)
    return {'coat_broad_adj':adjacency,'coat_brown_adj':brown_adjacency,'coat_curved':curved}

# Organic investigation v2 (train only)

No validation images or passes used; no classify.py/NOTES.md edits. All numeric choices are geometric/material design choices, with no searches or fitted coefficients. `organic_v2.py` provides `organic_features_v2(rgb)` returning `dog_face` and `saw_bar_housing`. Both remain experimental weak cues; I do not recommend dog_face in the final classifier.

Teacher consulted first through existing architecture/API and `organic_analysis.py`: three sorted images per organic class, original/grayscale/blur/vertical flip, reading post-ReLU activations and output classifications. Fish originals all classify correctly; grayscale and blur each destroy all three decisions. Dogs survive all three grayscale interventions, and blur on those examples largely preserves their class. Saws preserve grayscale decisions while blur destroys all three. This motivates colour+fine detail for fish, coarse colour-patch geometry for dog, and narrow material contours for saw; it does not authorize copying any response value.

Additional targeted teacher probes in `organic_v2_teacher.py`: two true saws with high new geometric score retain saw under grayscale but both become golf under blur. One retains a quarter-turn, one becomes horn. Highest-scoring false saw bar (`cassette_player/n02979186_10568`) remains cassette under grayscale and quarter-turn and becomes golf under blur. False bar church (`church/n03028079_2023`) remains church originally and after quarter-turn; gray becomes saw and blur parachute. The teacher therefore uses arrangements beyond the analytic bar detector, and bar evidence must be weak. High dog-face dog (`english_springer/n02102040_3916`) is dog original and blur, golf after grayscale/quarter-turn. Highest false dog-face pump (`gas_pump/n03425413_13298`) remains pump original/gray, golf blurred, parachute quarter-turned. Rectilinear apparatus genuinely mimics the broad ear/muzzle material layout.

Training measurements over all 505 images (feature diagnosis, no trained classifier accuracy):

- Existing broad white-fur texture and warm-white adjacency fail to separate dog reliably from horns/pumps. White-material fine-residual medians: dog .018, saw .020, horn .016, pump .017. Brown/dark-near-white medians: dog .021, horn .025, pump .019. Do not promote these alone.
- Existing Hough bar-pair feature fails: church median .878, saw .858, fish .840, dog .775, cassette .629. Do not use it as strong saw evidence.
- Strict green context (`g>r+.025 and g>b+.04`) does separate fish from close-up dogs in this training set: medians fish .172, golf .208, dog .003, saw .010, church .011. Olive alone fails: fish .283, dog .259. A fish rule should combine olive, strict green context, and smooth olive material, then reject golf using white round objects. These are diagnostic medians, not classifier parameters.
- Experimental frontal dog face scans four independently chosen window widths (40/64/96/128 at 160 square), requiring warm outer ears, central pale vertical blaze and lower dark nose. At diagnostic score >.15: dogs 27/50; false positives saw 24/50, church 24/55, horn 23/50, fish 12/50, pump 13/50, cassette 9/50, truck 11/50, golf 9/50, parachute 3/50. The largest score is a pump. **Reject this feature**, despite its plausible semantic account.
- Experimental saw bar attached to orange housing, naive version (parallel neutral midpoint, endpoint orange): diagnostic >.03 fires saw 37/50 but also fish 32/50, horn 29/50, church 26/55, pump 25/50, etc. Rejected.
- Requiring sustained neutral-bright interior and dark chain at both borders reduces diagnostic >.03 to saw 15/50, church 8/55, truck 7/50, cassette 6/50, horn 5/50, pump 4/50, parachute 4/50, golf 2/50, fish 1/50, dog 0/50.
- Finally requiring orange to be localised at a bar end relative to its centre gives saw 13/50, church 7/55, cassette 5/50, horn 5/50, truck 5/50, parachute 3/50, pump 2/50, fish 1/50, golf 1/50, dog 0/50. Precision is only 13/47, so **optional weak corroboration only**; it cannot drive a strong saw rule. This is the current `organic_v2.py` version.

Causal effect of adding necessary material conditions: the initial unconstrained bar has 37 saw vs >200 false positives at diagnostic >.03, while bright-metal + dark-chain + endpoint-localisation cuts false detections to 34 and retains 13 saw detections. There is class separation, but insufficient high-precision coverage. This is a falsified detector hypothesis, not an accuracy improvement claim. `organic_v2_probe.py` reproduces the final full-train feature counts; there are no stored feature tables in classifier code.

Recommended parent action: keep the simple coherent orange-housing colour clue, use the green/olive/smoothness conjunction for fish, and rely on nonrectilinear alternating coarse coat patches for dogs; do not add frontal dogface or raw bar-pair scores. The more constrained bar feature may be retained for later comparison, but I would spend validation on broader segmentation/context strategies instead.

Follow-up requested by root: broad white-patch morphology (about seven percent width) has a better semantic basis for rejecting narrow horn highlights. Added `broad_coat_features(rgb)` to the same separate module. It returns broad pale/dark adjacency, broad pale/muted-brown adjacency, and a contour conjunction measuring resolved pale area, local warm-brown exterior ring, and nonaxis outline share. Broad white is opened by an 11-pixel ellipse at 160 square, exterior neighbourhood has the same scale, and central seventy percent is used to discount distant borders. These choices express image geometry, not fitted values.

Full train feature measurements in `coat_probe.py`: curved warm-ring broad-white conjunction median dog .0093, pump .0018, truck .0017, fish .0006, saw .0001, church/horn/cassette/golf/parachute 0. Horn upper fifth .0243 overlaps dog .0322, so it remains corroboration rather than a standalone detector.

One explicitly proposed classifier-rule comparison, `coat_effect.py`: start with frozen `classify_v03.py`, replace its two generic dark/brown-near-white votes by two broad-patch adjacency votes. A visible two-percent image adjacency saturates one semantic unit; this is a chosen material-area meaning, not a fitted cutoff. Accuracy is **191/505 = 37.82%**, compared with **185/505 = 36.63%** for v03. This six-image change is smaller than a full-set standard error and is not strong accuracy evidence. Per-class before->after correct: fish18->18, dog24->22, cassette27->27, saw6->6, church23->25, horn13->15, truck20->21, pump16->17, golf14->15, parachute24->25. Predicted dogs84->60: horns miscalled dogs16->7, saw10->5, while true dog sensitivity24->22. This causally confirms less glint/trim confusion but trades away some dogs. No validation consumed. Root should record this measurement under an experimental v03+coat candidate if it is integrated or compared.

# Hypothesis: pink skin beside a central muted olive body and a finite horizontal body contrast distinguish held fish from grass, brown fur and brass.
from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image
import numpy as np, cv2
from collections import defaultdict

def fish_shapes(rgb):
 a=cv2.resize(rgb,(160,160)).astype(np.float32)/255
 r,g,b=a.transpose(2,0,1);gray=a.mean(2);spread=a.max(2)-a.min(2)
 olive=(np.minimum(r,g)>b+.035)&(abs(r-g)<.12)&(gray>.13)&(gray<.70)
 fishcolor=olive&(r>g-.025)&(r<g+.08)
 skin=(r>g*1.15)&(g>b*1.05)&(b>g*.65)&(r>.45)&(gray>.30)&(spread<.40)
 nearbody=cv2.GaussianBlur(fishcolor.astype(np.float32),(0,0),8)
 out=[skin.mean(),(skin*nearbody).mean(),fishcolor.mean()]
 # Analytic finite ellipse/surround filters test several body fractions rather than templates learned from photographs.
 best=0.;best2=0.;best3=0.
 for width in (48,80,112):
  rad=width//2; yy,xx=np.mgrid[-rad:rad+1,-rad:rad+1].astype(float)
  for angle in (0,np.pi/6,-np.pi/6):
   u=xx*np.cos(angle)+yy*np.sin(angle);v=-xx*np.sin(angle)+yy*np.cos(angle)
   inside=(u/(width/2))**2+(v/(width/6))**2<1
   ring=((u/(width/2))**2+(v/(width/3))**2<1)&~inside
   kernel=inside.astype(np.float32)/max(inside.sum(),1)-ring.astype(np.float32)/max(ring.sum(),1)
   contrast=cv2.filter2D(fishcolor.astype(np.float32),-1,kernel)
   # Patch support is required as well as contrast; reflected padding avoided by central pooling.
   average=cv2.filter2D(fishcolor.astype(np.float32),-1,inside.astype(np.float32)/max(inside.sum(),1))
   pink=cv2.GaussianBlur(skin.astype(np.float32),(0,0),width/5)
   best=max(best,float((np.maximum(contrast,0)*average)[24:136,24:136].max()))
   best2=max(best2,float((np.maximum(contrast,0)*average*pink)[24:136,24:136].max()))
   best3=max(best3,float((average*pink)[24:136,24:136].max()))
 out.extend([best,best2,best3])
 return out
rows=defaultdict(list)
for p in sorted(Path('data/train').glob('*/*.JPEG')):rows[p.parent.name].append(fish_shapes(np.asarray(Image.open(p).convert('RGB'))))
for c,v in rows.items():print(c,'median',np.round(np.median(v,axis=0),4),'upper',np.round(np.quantile(v,.8,axis=0),4))
